title: Shake and Spill: Half-Life
subject: physical science
goal: Find out how a pile of atoms decays when each atom's decay is pure chance, and explain what a half-life is.
steps: Cut out the 60 atoms. Each is printed on one side only. Record round 0: 60 atoms left.
Put the atoms in a cup, shake it, and spill them on the desk. Every atom that lands blank side up has decayed: move it to the decayed pile.
Count the atoms still printed side up. The Recorder writes it in the table; the Skeptic counts again.
Put only the atoms that are left back in the cup. Pass the role cards to the left.
Repeat until fewer than 3 atoms are left. Then, together: about how many spills does it take for half of the atoms to decay?
listen_for: Expecting exactly half each spill. Ask: what would “exactly half” of 7 atoms be?
Thinking an atom that survived many spills is “due” to decay. Each spill is a fresh chance for every atom.
The Skeptic asking how the group knows its count is right.
debrief: Put every group's counts on the board and add them up for each spill. The class total halves much more evenly than any one group's: ask why.
Carbon-14's half-life is 5,730 years. Ask: if one spill stood for one half-life, how old is a bone after three spills?
sources: Inspired by the classic coin-flip half-life activity, an idea also modeled in PhET Interactive Simulations' Radioactive Dating Game (University of Colorado Boulder). The activity and questions were written for Paper Loop.
